newsitem.title: USA: U.S. appeal ban cannot be retroactive - high court.
newsitem.headline: U.S. appeal ban cannot be retroactive - high court.

text.p: The Supreme Court ruled Monday that a federal law sharply restricting appeals by most prisoners applied only to cases brought after President Clinton signed the legislation last year.

By a 5-4 vote, the justices said the law, which limits federal court appeals by inmates who have received a sentence other than the death penalty, should not apply to cases that were pending when Clinton signed it in April 1996.

The contested provision limited the issues a federal court might consider in non-death-penalty cases. It effectively barred an appeal on any claim already decided on its merits, as opposed to procedural grounds, in state court proceedings.

The case before the Supreme Court involved Aaron Lindh, found guilty of two murders in a 1988 shooting in Madison, Wisc., and sentenced to two consecutive life sentences plus 35 years. He challenged his conviction, saying his constitutional rights had been violated because his lawyer had been barred from asking about allegations a key prosecution witness, a psychiatrist, had had sexual relations with his patients.

The Wisconsin Supreme Court upheld his conviction and Lindh then brought a federal habeas appeal. He appealed to the Supreme Court after a U.S. appeals court ruled that the restrictions in the 1996 federal law applied retroactively and Lindh could not pursue his appeal.

Justice David Souter said in the majority opinion that the appeals court was wrong. He said the law's other provisions applied only to cases after it became effective and the same principle should govern pending non-death-penalty cases.
